title: The plain honesty of the Gospel writers
source_text: Τὰ δ᾿ ἑξῆς τοῦ Κέλσου κατανοητέον. ἐν οἷς καὶ ἡμῖν φησι πίστιν ποιεῖν προκαταλαβοῦσαν ἡμῶν τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοιάνδε συγκατάθεσιν. ἀληθῶς (μὲν) γὰρ πίστις ἡμῖν ποιεῖ τὴν τοιαύτην συγκατάθεσιν· ὅρα δὲ εἰ μὴ αὐτόθεν ἡ πίστις αὐτὴ τὸ ἐπαινετὸν παρίστησιν, ὅτε πιστεύομεν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ, χάριν ὁμολογοῦντες τῷ εἰς τοιαύτην πίστιν ὁδηγῷ καὶ λέγοντες αὐτὸν οὐκ ἀθεεὶ τὸ τηλικοῦτον τετολμηκέναι καὶ ἠνυκέναι· πιστεύομεν δὲ καὶ ταῖς προαιρέσεσι τῶν γραψάντων τὰ εὐαγγέλια. καταστοχαζόμενοι τῆς εὐλαβείας αὐτῶν καὶ τοῦ συνειδότος, ἐμφαινομένων τοῖς γράμμασιν, οὐδὲν νόθον καὶ κυβευτικὸν καὶ πεπλασμένον καὶ πανοῦργον ἐχόντων, καὶ γὰρ παρίσταται ἡμῖν οτι οὐκ ἂν ψυχαὶ, μὴ μαθοῦσαι τὰ τοιαῦτα. ὁποῖα διδάσκει ἡ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι πανοῦργος σοφιστεία, πολλὴν ἔχουσα τὴν πιθανότητα καὶ τὴν ὀξύτητα. καὶ ἡ ἐν τοῖς δικαστηρίοις καλινδουμένη ῥητορικὴ. οὕτως πλάσαι οἷοί τ᾿ ἦσαν πράγματα, δυνάμενα ἀφ᾿ αὑτῶν ἔχειν τὸ πρὸς πίστιν καὶ τὸν ἀνάλογον τῇ πίστει βίον ἀγωγόν. οἶμαι δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἰησοῦν διὰ τοῦτο βεβουλῆσθαι διδασκάλοις τοῦ δόγματος χρῆσθαι τοιούτοις, ἵνα μηδεμίαν μὲν ἔχῃ χώραν ὑπόνοια πιθανῶν σοφισμάτων, λαμπρῶς δὲ τοῖς συνιέναι δυναμένοις ἐμφαίνηται ὅτι τὸ ἄδολον τῆς προαιρέσεως τῶν γραψάντων, ἐχούσης πολὺ τὸ, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, ἀφελὲς, ἠξιώθη θειοτέρας δυνάμεως, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἀνυούσης ἤπερ ἀνύειν δύνασθαι δοκεῖ περιβολὴ λόγων καὶ λέξεων σύνθεσις καὶ μετὰ διαιρέσεων καὶ τεχνολογίας Ἑλληνικῆς ἀκολουθία.
pass_a_gloss: The next things of Celsus must be considered (κατανοητέον), in which he says (φησι) that for us too faith (πίστις), having taken hold beforehand of our soul, makes such assent (συγκατάθεσις) about Jesus. For truly faith makes such assent for us; but see whether faith itself does not straightway (αὐτόθεν) present the praiseworthy (ἐπαινετόν), when we entrust (πιστεύω) ourselves to the God over all, confessing thanks to the guide (ὁδηγός) into such faith and saying that not without God (οὐκ ἀθεεί) did he dare (τολμάω) and accomplish (ἀνύω) so great a thing. And we trust (πιστεύω) the choices/intentions (προαιρέσεις) of those who wrote the Gospels (εὐαγγέλια), conjecturing/inferring (καταστοχάζομαι) their piety/reverence (εὐλάβεια) and conscience (συνειδός) appearing (ἐμφαίνομαι) in the writings (γράμματα), [they] having nothing spurious (νόθος), dice-player's/cheating (κυβευτικός), fabricated (πεπλασμένος), or knavish (πανοῦργος). For it is evident to us that souls not having learned such things as the knavish sophistry (σοφιστεία) among Greeks teaches, having much persuasiveness (πιθανότης) and sharpness (ὀξύτης), and the rhetoric (ῥητορική) rolling about (καλινδέομαι) in law courts (δικαστήρια), would not thus have been able to fabricate (πλάσσω) matters (πράγματα) able of themselves to have what [leads] to faith and the life analogous (ἀνάλογος) to faith leading (ἀγωγός). And I think Jesus too for this reason willed (βούλομαι) to use such teachers of the doctrine (δόγμα), so that suspicion (ὑπόνοια) of persuasive sophisms (σοφίσματα) might have no room (χώρα), and it might appear brightly (λαμπρῶς) to those able to understand (συνίημι) that the guilelessness (τὸ ἄδολον) of the intention of the writers, having much of, so to name it, simplicity (ἀφελές), was deemed worthy (ἀξιόω) of a more divine power, accomplishing much more than elaboration of speech (περιβολὴ λόγων), composition of words, and sequence (ἀκολουθία) with divisions (διαιρέσεις) and Greek technical method (τεχνολογία) is thought able to accomplish.
pass_b_english: We must now consider what Celsus says next. In it he says that with us too it is faith, having taken hold of our soul beforehand, that produces this kind of assent concerning Jesus. Faith does truly produce such assent in us. But see whether faith itself does not at once show what is praiseworthy in it, when we entrust ourselves to the God who is over all, giving thanks to the one who led us to such faith, and saying that it was not without God that he dared and achieved so great a thing.

We also trust the intentions of those who wrote the Gospels, discerning their reverence and their conscience, which show in their writings, for they have nothing spurious about them, nothing of the gambler's tricks, nothing made up and nothing crafty. For it is clear to us that souls which had not learned the sort of things taught by the crafty sophistry of the Greeks, which has great persuasiveness and sharpness, and by the rhetoric that wallows in the law courts, would not have been able to invent in this way matters that could carry in themselves what leads to faith and to a life in keeping with that faith.

I think too that this is why Jesus chose to use such men as teachers of his doctrine: so that there might be no room for any suspicion of plausible sophistries, and so that it might shine out plainly to those able to understand that the guilelessness of the writers' intention, which had in it much of what I may call simplicity, was counted worthy of a more divine power, a power that achieves far more than elaborate speech, the arrangement of words, and an argument that proceeds by divisions and the technical methods of the Greeks are thought able to achieve.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 39 (Koetschau 3.39). Celsus's claim is reported indirectly (φησι + infinitive) and is not set in quotation marks. (μέν) is an editorial supplement. The 'guide into such faith' and the one who 'dared and achieved' are Jesus. οὐκ ἀθεεί ('not without God') is a Homeric phrase (Odyssey 18.353) that Origen uses as a set expression; it is not marked as a quotation. The staged punctuation in the middle sentence (full stops after τοιαῦτα and ῥητορική) breaks one long sentence; the translation follows the grammar, taking ψυχαί as subject of οἷοί τ' ἦσαν πλάσαι. ἐχόντων is taken with the writers (αὐτῶν); it could also be read with their reverence and conscience as shown in the writings, with no change of sense. Possible allusion, not cited inline: 1 Corinthians 2:1-5 (preaching not in persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration of power), which this argument resembles but does not quote.
οὐκ ἀθεεί: 'it was not without God that he dared and achieved so great a thing' (natural English order; negation unchanged)
δοκεῖ ἀνύειν δύνασθαι: 'are thought able to achieve' (was 'can seem able')
Celsus's claim kept as indirect speech, no quotation marks; no Scripture cited inline (1 Corinthians 2:1-5 only a possible echo, noted)
